# Context

**Big picture:**

  - Wildland fuels are the combustible biomass that fuels wildland fires. Fuels 
  are often divided into several types of "fuel components" (e.g. duff, litter, 
  fine woody debris, coarse woody debris, understory vegetation, canopy fuels).
  - Current operational (i.e., useful for predicting fires in real time) fire 
  models ignore fine-scale heterogeneity in fuel conditions, and predict fire 
  behavior using basic summary statistics (e.g. mean biomass per area) for 
  the modeled area (often a 30x30m pixel). Computational 
  fluid dynamics models are fire models that do include fine-scale heterogeneity 
  in fuel conditions and atmosphere/fire feedbacks, but run slower than real 
  time and so are useful mostly for research.
  - Research and theory suggest that fine-scale heterogeneity in fuel conditions 
  does affect fire behavior at coarser scales
  - We've been funded by the Pyregence consortium to develop a system for 
  sampling and describing fuel conditions that will supply input data for 
  a new fire model in development by researchers at the US Forest Service. The 
  new model is to incorporate fine-scale heterogeneity in fuel conditions, among 
  other innovations. 
  - The ultimate goal is to develop a system for field sampling and data analysis 
  that will capture information about the fine-scale spatial distribution of 
  combustible biomass to enable realistic predictions of wildfire behavior. 
  - Ideally, we would like to accomplish this goal by developing spatially-explicit 
  statistical models for different fuel components (e.g. litter, woody 
  debris, understory vegetation). By defining a common statistical model and 
  allowing the parameters to vary by ecosystem, we could generate simulated 
  fuelbeds with realistic spatial properties for input into the fire model. A 
  parametric statistical model also opens up avenues for research, such as comparisons 
  among ecosystems. 
  - As a fallback, the sampling design is intended to allow for directly using 
  the observed data to map fuel conditions at a fine scale. We could plug the 
  observed data into the fire model directly, skipping the statistical analysis and 
  simulation steps. This may be necessary for some fuel components which are 
  difficult to model well. In a mixture of the two approaches, kriging would be used to 
  fill the spatial gaps between observations for some fuel components. 

**This paper:**

  - I'm also interested in the fine-scale spatial pattern of biomass as an 
  important and understudied axis of forest structure. Fire is an important 
  ecological process in the ecosystem I study (Californian mixed conifer 
  forests), and research shows that fire alters the loading (amount) of biomass 
  of several fuel components. My hypothesis is that fire will also alter the 
  fine-scale spatial distribution of biomass.
  - We used a prescribed fire study happening and Blodgett Forest Research 
  Station as a test-bed for the sampling protocol and spatial statistical 
  analysis we're delivering for the pyregence grant. By sampling and 
  describing the fine-scale spatial pattern of fuels before and after a 
  prescribed fire treatment, we can also test whether the prescribed fire 
  affects the fine-scale spatial pattern.
  - This paper will focus on duff, litter, and fine woody debris (FWD), which are the 
  fuel components most strongly affected by prescribed fires and the easiest 
  to model. 

# Data collection

  - 19 inventory plots were spread across 3 experimental units (. Plots were 
  placed on an existing grid used by the research forest:
  
```{r echo = FALSE}
ggplot()+
  geom_sf(data = burn_units, fill = NA,
         aes(color = 'Experimental units'), lwd = 1)+
  geom_sf(data = plot_centers,
          aes(color = 'Plot centers'))+
  theme_minimal()+
  #ggspatial::annotation_scale()+
  scale_color_manual(values = c('Plot centers' = 'red',
                                'Experimental units' = 'black'))+
  theme(legend.title = element_blank())+
  coord_sf(datum = sf::st_crs('EPSG:26910'))+
  labs(x = 'Easting (m)', y = 'Northing (m)')

```

  - On each plot:
    - The depth of litter and duff was measured (to nearest 0.5 cm) at 64 
    predetermined subsample locations.
    - FWD particles (in 3 size classes) intersecting 
    a 1m subtransect were counted at 32 predetermined subsample locations.
  - The spatial arrangements of subsample locations within each plot were 
  designed to get good coverage of pairwise distances between subsamples in 
  the range 0.1m - 60m for litter/duff and the range 1m-60m for FWD. Variogram 
  analysis from other forest and rangeland ecosystems in the western US 
  suggests that most spatial correlation is within a distance of ~1m for 
  litter/duff and within ~5m for FWD. Here are histograms of the pairwise 
  distances for a single plot:

```{r echo = FALSE}
dist(litter_data$coords) %>% as.matrix() %>% as.vector() %>% 
  hist(main = 'Histogram of Litter/duff subsample pairwise distances')

dist(fwd1h_data$coords) %>% as.matrix() %>% as.vector() %>% 
  hist(main = 'Historgam of FWD subsample pariwise distances')

```

  - Fuels were inventoried both before and after prescribed burns of the 
  three experimental units. The three burns took place on separate days.

# Data exploration

## Duff

Histogram of duff depths, rounded to the nearest cm:

```{r}
duff_data$X %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(depth_cm = duff_data$Y) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = depth_cm))+
  geom_bar()+
  theme_minimal()+
  labs(title = 'Duff')

```

Boxplot crossing timestep (pre/post burn) with experimental unit (A, B, or C):

```{r}


duff_data$X %>%
  as_tibble() %>%
  mutate(depth_cm = duff_data$Y,
         timestep = 
           factor(ifelse(timePost==0,'pre', 'post'),
                  levels = c('pre', 'post')),
         comp = ifelse(compB==0&compC==0,
                       'A',
                       ifelse(compB==1,
                              'B',
                              'C'))) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = depth_cm))+
  geom_bar()+
  facet_grid(timestep~comp, scales = 'free_y')+
  theme_minimal()+
  labs(title = 'Duff')

```

# Analysis

## Model Descriptions

### Litter+duff depths

The model for litter and/or duff depths is:

$$Y_i \sim \text{NegBinomial}(\mu_i, \kappa)$$

where:

  - $Y_i$ is the observed depth of litter or duff at observation $i$ in 
  centimeters, rounded to the nearest cm
  - $\mu_i$ is the unobserved mean depth at observation $i$
  - $\kappa$ is the negative binomial dispersion parameter, here assumed constant 
  across all samples
  
$$\text{log}(\mu_i) = \textbf{X}_i\beta + \textbf{GPPRE}_{l,p} IPRE_i + 
\textbf{GPPOST}_{l,p} IPOST_i +b_{p}$$

where:

  - $\textbf{X}_i$ is the *i*th row of the design matrix of fixed effects covariates.
  The fixed effects covariates are for experimental unit (A, B, or C) crossed 
  with timestep (pre or post), so there are 6 main effects (Intercept = A:Pre,
  main effect B, main effect C, main effect Post, B:Post,  and C:Post).
  - $\beta$ are the 6 coefficients for the fixed effects
  - $\textbf{GPPRE}$ is an $L\times P$ matrix of realized gaussian process random effects, 
  with $L$ rows for the within-plot spatial locations and $P$ columns 
  for the plots. $l$ is the index of the location for the 
  observation $i$ and $p$ is the index for the plot of of the observation $i$. 
  - $IPRE_i$ is a dummy variable (1 if true, 0 if false) coding 
  whether observation *i* is from the preburn timestep and controlling whether 
  the pre-burn gaussian process random effect $\textbf{GPPRE}_{l_i,p_i}$ is 
  included in the linear predictor $\mu_i$.
  - $\textbf{GPPOST}$ and $IPOST_i$ are likewise the matrix of 
  gaussian process random effects and an indicator variable for the postburn 
  timestep. 
  - $b$ is a vector of normally distributed random effects for the plots, 
  $b \sim \text{Normal}(0,\sigma_{plot}^2)$, and $b_{p}$ is the random effect 
  for plot $p$, the plot associated with observation $i$.
  
$$\textbf{GPPRE}_{1:L,p} \sim \text{MVN}(0,\Sigma_{PRE})$$

where:

  - $\Sigma_{PRE}$ is the $L$ by $L$ covariance matrix of sample locations within 
  a plot. The gaussian process parameters, and thus the covariance matrix, 
  are constant across plots. 
  
$$\Sigma_{PRE} = \alpha_{PRE}^2 \text{exp}(\frac{-D^2}{2\rho_{PRE}^2})$$

where:

  - $\alpha_{PRE}$ is the standard deviation of the gaussian process random 
  effect for the preburn timestep, controlling the magnitude of the spatial effect
  - $D^2$ is the $L$ by $L$ matrix of squared distances among all sample locations
  in a plot
  - $\rho_{PRE}$ is the length-scale parameter of the gaussian process random effect 
  the breburn timestep, 
  controlling the rate at which the correlation between observations decays 
  as the distance between them increases

The definitions for $\textbf{GPPOST}$, $\Sigma_{POST}$, $\alpha_{POST}$, and 
$\rho_{POST}$ are as above.

Stan code for Litter+duff model:

```{stan, eval = FALSE, output.var = 'litterduff_model'}


data {
  int N; // number of observations
  int P; // number of plots
  int L; // number of distinct locations within each plot
  
  int Y[N]; // observed responses
  int plot_id[N]; // plot IDs
  int location_id[N]; // location IDs
  
  matrix[N,6] X; // fixed effects design matrix, giving dummy variables for 
                 // COMP (A, B, or C) crossed with TIMESTEP (pre and post), with 
                 // A:PRE the intercept
  
  int pre[N]; // indicator 1 if pre 0 if post
  int post[N]; // timestep explanatory variable; 1 if post, 0 otherwise
  
  vector[2] coords[L]; // plot-relative coordinates of each subsample
}

parameters {
  vector[6] beta; // fixed effect coefficients 
  matrix[L,P] zGP_pre; // standard-normal deviates for GP effect prefire
  matrix[L,P] zGP_post; // standard normal deviates for GP effect postfire
  
  real<lower=0> alpha_pre; // standard deviation of prefire GP
  real<lower=0> rho_pre; // length-scales of prefire GP
  
  real<lower=0> alpha_post; // standard deviation of postfire GP
  real<lower=0> rho_post; // length-scale of postfire GP
  
  real<lower=0> sigmaPlot; // standard deviation of plot effect
  vector[P] z_plot; // standard normal deviates for plot effect
  
  real<lower=0> kappa; // NB dispersion parameter
  
}

transformed parameters {

  vector[P] plot_effect; // atual plot effects
  

  plot_effect = sigmaPlot * z_plot;
}

model {
  // variable declarations
  vector[N] logmu; // linear predictor
  matrix[L,P] GP_pre; // actual GP effects for each plot:location
  matrix[L,P] GP_post; // actual GP effects for postfire
  matrix[L,L] K_pre; // covariance matrix for within-plot GP (prefire)
  matrix[L,L] KL_pre; // cholesky decomposition of K_pre
  matrix[L,L] K_post; // covariance matrix for within-plot GP (postfire)
  matrix[L,L] KL_post; // cholesky decomposition of K_post
  
  // priors
  beta ~ normal(0, 5);
  sigmaPlot ~ normal(0, 5);
  kappa ~ cauchy(0,5);
  alpha_pre ~ normal(0, 5);
  alpha_post ~ normal(0, 5);
  rho_pre ~ inv_gamma(5,40);
  rho_post ~ inv_gamma(5,40);
  
  // random effect realizations
  z_plot ~ std_normal();
  to_vector(zGP_pre) ~ std_normal();
  to_vector(zGP_post) ~ std_normal();
  
  // gaussian processse
  K_pre = gp_exp_quad_cov(coords, alpha_pre, rho_pre);
  K_pre = add_diag(K_pre, 1e-9);
  KL_pre = cholesky_decompose(K_pre);
  GP_pre = KL_pre * zGP_pre;
  
  K_post = gp_exp_quad_cov(coords, alpha_post, rho_post);
  K_post = add_diag(K_post, 1e-9);
  KL_post = cholesky_decompose(K_post);
  GP_post = KL_post * zGP_post;
  
  // linear predictor
  for (i in 1:N){
    logmu[i] = 
      X[i,] * beta +
      GP_pre[location_id[i], plot_id[i]] * pre[i] +
      GP_post[location_id[i], plot_id[i]] * post[i] +
      plot_effect[plot_id[i]];
  }
  
  // likelihood
  Y ~ neg_binomial_2_log(logmu, kappa);
}

```

### FWD counts

The model for FWD counts is identical to that for litter+duff depths, except 
that

$$\Sigma_{PRE} = \alpha_{PRE}^2 \text{exp}(\frac{-D^2}{2\rho_{PRE}^2})+\textbf{I}\tau_{PRE}$$

where:

  - $\Sigma_{PRE}$, $\alpha_{PRE}$, $D$, and $\rho_{PRE}$ are as defined for the 
  litter+duff model
  - $\textbf{I}$ is an $L \times L$ identify matrix with 1s on the diagonal and 
  0s otherwise
  - $\tau_{PRE}$ is the noise parameter for the gaussian process random effect, 
  controlling the covariance between samples which share a common location.
  
$\Sigma_{POST}$ likewise has its own noise parameter $\tau_{POST}$.

Stan code for the FWD model:

```{stan, eval = FALSE, output.var = 'fwd_model'}

data {
  int N; // number of observations
  int P; // number of plots
  int L; // number of distinct locations within each plot
  
  int Y[N]; // observed responses
  int plot_id[N]; // plot IDs
  int location_id[N]; // location IDs
  
  matrix[N,6] X; // fixed effects design matrix, giving dummy variables for 
                 // COMP (A, B, or C) crossed with TIMESTEP (pre and post), with 
                 // A:PRE the intercept
  
  int pre[N]; // indicator 1 if pre 0 if post
  int post[N]; // timestep explanatory variable; 1 if post, 0 otherwise
  
  vector[2] coords[L]; // plot-relative coordinates of each subsample
}

parameters {
  vector[6] beta; // fixed effect coefficients 
  matrix[L,P] zGP_pre; // standard-normal deviates for GP effect prefire
  matrix[L,P] zGP_post; // standard normal deviates for GP effect postfire
  
  real<lower=0> alpha_pre; // standard deviation of prefire GP
  real<lower=0> rho_pre; // length-scales of prefire GP
  real<lower=0> tau_pre;
  
  real<lower=0> alpha_post; // standard deviation of postfire GP
  real<lower=0> rho_post; // length-scale of postfire GP
  real<lower=0> tau_post;
  
  real<lower=0> sigmaPlot; // standard deviation of plot effect
  vector[P] z_plot; // standard normal deviates for plot effect
  
  real<lower=0> kappa; // NB dispersion parameter
  
}

transformed parameters {

  vector[P] plot_effect; // atual plot effects
  

  plot_effect = sigmaPlot * z_plot;
}

model {
  // variable declarations
  vector[N] logmu; // linear predictor
  matrix[L,P] GP_pre; // actual GP effects for each plot:location
  matrix[L,P] GP_post; // actual GP effects for postfire
  matrix[L,L] K_pre; // covariance matrix for within-plot GP (prefire)
  matrix[L,L] KL_pre; // cholesky decomposition of K_pre
  matrix[L,L] K_post; // covariance matrix for within-plot GP (postfire)
  matrix[L,L] KL_post; // cholesky decomposition of K_post
  
  // priors
  beta ~ normal(0, 2);
  sigmaPlot ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  kappa ~ cauchy(0,5);
  alpha_pre ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  alpha_post ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  rho_pre ~ inv_gamma(5,40);
  rho_post ~ inv_gamma(5,40);
  tau_pre ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  tau_post ~ normal(0, 0.5);
  
  // random effect realizations
  z_plot ~ std_normal();
  to_vector(zGP_pre) ~ std_normal();
  to_vector(zGP_post) ~ std_normal();
  
  // gaussian processse
  K_pre = gp_exp_quad_cov(coords, alpha_pre, rho_pre);
  K_pre = add_diag(K_pre, tau_pre);
  KL_pre = cholesky_decompose(K_pre);
  GP_pre = KL_pre * zGP_pre;
  
  K_post = gp_exp_quad_cov(coords, alpha_post, rho_post);
  K_post = add_diag(K_post, tau_post);
  KL_post = cholesky_decompose(K_post);
  GP_post = KL_post * zGP_post;
  
  // linear predictor
  for (i in 1:N){
    logmu[i] = 
      X[i,] * beta +
      GP_pre[location_id[i], plot_id[i]] * pre[i] +
      GP_post[location_id[i], plot_id[i]] * post[i] +
      plot_effect[plot_id[i]];
  }
  
  // likelihood
  Y ~ neg_binomial_2_log(logmu, kappa);
}



```
